Something that came to mind regarding the elevator operator. The elevators requiring an operator versus an automated operator, is quite different. When the transition happened likely less so, but still more similar to what we have today than what if replaced. Platform shift, think horses to automobiles. Large platform shifts, are more disruptive than more automation to the same platform. AI, that exists currently is still the same platform. Drastically changes the job, but evaluating code written by AI that is the same operating systems and programming languages, is different than shifting to something like quantum computers (speaking from ignorance with specifics to quantum, hopefully the metaphor is present at least). Really curious to know how many elevator operators became elevator technicians. While on the surface, their job doesn't immediately make you imagine someone working on the elevator. Some number of them, that were excellent at their job, likely fixed a lot of problems they dealt with regarding the elevator. While the platform shift is much more disruptive, and elevator operator is the example that did go away (according to this the only in the time period evaluated). What the data isn't likely to spell out, is what number of those operators became technicians. Some individuals, as they said the peak of demand for the job, likely did the job well, and was close to the job, and close to the physical place that the new platform came in as the thing they knew well went out. I'm curious how many curious individuals with the opportunity was amongst the last batch of elevator operators and the first ever, elevator technicians. Curious if others had the same thought.

I'm using chatGPT to counter argue Max's thesis: The historical record shows that automation can create new work while still permanently lowering the income, security, and bargaining power of many displaced workers—and AI may intensify that pattern because it can automate broad chains of cognitive work faster than equivalent new human roles emerge. 1. **AI Is Broader Than Past Automation** Past technologies usually automated one narrow task: ATMs dispensed cash, spreadsheets calculated numbers, and nail guns drove nails. AI can potentially perform many different cognitive tasks across many occupations using the same underlying technology, so the historical analogy may break. 2. **Jobs Can Survive While Employment Collapses** An occupation does not have to disappear for employment in it to fall sharply. If one AI-enabled accountant, programmer, lawyer, or analyst can do the work that previously required several people, the profession survives while the number of people needed in it drops. 3. **Productivity Does Not Guarantee More Demand** Automation creates more employment only when lower costs or better capabilities generate enough new demand to absorb the labor saved. Airlines could expand enormously as aviation became more efficient, but companies may not want five times as much accounting, legal analysis, HR reporting, or software maintenance just because AI makes those activities cheaper. 4. **Automation Has a Real Displacement Effect** Economic research distinguishes between technology that augments workers and technology that substitutes capital for human tasks. Historically, new human tasks often offset displacement, but there is no guarantee AI will create new human work as quickly as it automates existing work. 5. **The “60% of Jobs Are New” Statistic Ignores What Happened to the Workers Who Lost the Old Jobs** **Factory workers:** Many workers displaced from manufacturing from the 1960s through the 2000s did not move smoothly into equally good new careers. Large numbers ended up with lower earnings, weaker benefits, less job security, or outside the labor force altogether; the economy eventually created new jobs, but many of the original displaced workers experienced a lasting decline in living standards. **Clerical workers:** From the 1980s onward, PCs, spreadsheets, databases, email, ERP systems, and self-service software steadily reduced demand for secretaries, typists, bookkeepers, file clerks, and other administrative workers. Again, the economy created new kinds of work, but that did not mean the displaced clerical worker received an equivalent replacement career; many moved into lower-paid service work or left the occupation entirely. **Why it matters for AI:** Saying that new occupations eventually appear answers the aggregate economic question, not the worker's question. What matters to someone whose middle-class job disappears is whether they can move into the new economy without losing income, benefits, security, or occupational status—and past manufacturing and clerical transitions show that many workers could not. 6. **AI Could Hollow Out Career Ladders** Many professions train future experts by giving junior workers routine research, drafting, coding, analysis, and administrative work. If AI absorbs much of that entry-level work, firms may hire fewer juniors, eventually leaving fewer people with the experience needed to become tomorrow's senior professionals. 7. **“Someone Using AI Will Take Your Job” Actually Implies Displacement** If an AI-enabled employee becomes twice as productive, the employer may need only half as many employees unless demand also doubles. The author's own warning that AI users will replace non-users therefore contains a mechanism by which total employment can shrink. 8. **Huge Productivity Gains Strengthen the Displacement Case** The larger the productivity improvement from AI, the stronger the economic incentive to produce the same output with fewer workers. You cannot simultaneously argue that AI will make workers dramatically more productive and assume that firms will continue employing the same number of them. 9. **“AI Doesn't Replace the Hard Parts” May Only Describe AI Today** The boundary between routine and difficult work keeps moving. Translation, image creation, coding, document analysis, and complex information retrieval were all once regarded as relatively resistant to automation, so today's AI limitations are weak evidence about where that boundary will sit ten or twenty years from now. 10. **New Economic Activity May Itself Be Automated** AI may enable products and services that previously would never have existed, but those new activities do not necessarily create proportional human employment. An AI system could increasingly design a product, generate production instructions, market it, sell it, support customers, and coordinate automated manufacturing and logistics with relatively little labor. 11. **The Gains May Accrue More to Capital Than Labor** If more expertise becomes embedded in AI systems rather than workers, economic power can shift toward whoever owns the models, data, compute, platforms, and companies. Society could become substantially richer and more productive while simultaneously needing fewer workers and giving labor a smaller share of the resulting wealth. 12. **Even Successful Long-Term Adaptation Could Produce a Brutal Transition** Even if AI eventually creates as many jobs as it destroys, workers cannot instantly move between occupations, locations, skill levels, and industries. A 50-year-old displaced accountant or factory worker does not automatically become an AI engineer because the economy created a new occupation somewhere else; years of lower earnings, unemployment, retraining, and lost status can occur even if the long-run aggregate statistics eventually look healthy.
